interest: Candid 1939 report on Manchukuo monopolies, farmer and merchant grievances, and farm output still below 1930 levels.
overview: This file consists of Despatch No. 3497 (dated December 13, 1939) from American Consul William R. Langdon at the U.S. Consulate General in Mukden, Manchuria, to the Secretary of State, transmitting a comprehensive monthly economic report on conditions and developments in South Manchuria for November 1939. The report details the tightening Japanese wartime control over the economy of Manchukuo, highlighting trade statistics and the virtual collapse of exports to third countries outside the yen bloc. It covers new state monopolies and regulatory legislation governing staple produce (notably soybeans), important cereals (kaoliang, corn, millet), daily consumer necessities, and wheat flour milling. Additionally, the report reviews agricultural harvest forecasts impacted by autumn flooding, livestock control legislation, government subventions for seed distribution, the public offering of Manchuria Telegraph and Telephone Company shares, sumptuary taxes on entertainment, patent bureau statistics, industrial ventures including a bean-stalk rayon pulp mill in Kaiyuan and Mitsui mining expansions, and new strategic railway lines constructed to connect industrial mining centers and Soviet border areas.

subfiles.about: Monthly economic report detailing foreign trade, agricultural yields, commodity monopolies, state control laws, industrial developments, and railway extensions in South Manchuria during November 1939.
subfiles.from: Wm. R. Langdon, American Consul, Mukden
subfiles.summary: This report reviews economic conditions in South Manchuria for November 1939, highlighting the severe decline in exports to countries outside the yen bloc and expanding import restrictions. It details the establishment and enforcement of state monopolies over soybeans, staple cereals (kaoliang, corn, millet), daily necessities, and wheat milling designed to align Manchurian resources with Japanese domestic requirements. Agricultural harvest estimates reveal an overall decline attributed to autumn floods, with total yields remaining ten percent below 1930 levels despite Japanese development programs. The report also documents the passage of livestock adjustment legislation, government financing for seed distribution, the public sale of Manchuria Telegraph and Telephone Company shares, new luxury entertainment taxes, industrial projects such as a bean-stalk rayon pulp plant and Mitsui mining ventures, and the completion of two strategic railway lines connecting resource-rich zones and the Soviet frontier.
subfiles.title: Report on Economic Conditions and Developments in South Manchuria, November 1939
subfiles.to: Department of State, Washington (and diplomatic missions in Peiping, Chungking, Tokyo, Shanghai, Harbin, Dairen)
